title: MC0-09411
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated June 30, 2020, rejecting their refugee protection claims on the ground that the female appellant did not provide credible testimony.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The female appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and her adult children, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (associate appellants), are citizens of Mexico. They are appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated June 30, 2020, rejecting their refugee protection claims on the ground that the female appellant did not provide credible testimony.

The female appellant alleges that her spouse, who owned a XXXX business in Puebla, was kidnapped, held captive and released for ransom in XXXX 2014. This event is believed to be the work of the La Famille Michoacán [the Michoacán family] cartel. The entire family allegedly fled to the United States in XXXX 2014, but the female appellant and her daughter (the female associate appellant) returned to Mexico in XXXX 2014, while her son, the associate male appellant, remained in the United States with his father. During this time, the female appellant and her daughter allegedly stayed in San Francisco Del Rincón while making trips to Puebla.

All the family members were reunited in Puebla in XXXX 2016. However, the threats to, and extortion of the appellants allegedly resumed in XXXX 2017. They reportedly went into hiding in XXXX 2018, before fleeing the country to Canada in XXXX 2018 to claim refugee protection here. The female appellant's husband allegedly remained in hiding in Mexico and has little contact with his family in Canada.

The appellants are contesting five findings concerning the credibility of their allegations and are claiming a breach of procedural fairness due to the RPD's conclusions on documents about which they were not questioned. For the reasons that follow, the RAD is of the opinion that there was no breach of procedural fairness and that the RPD's decision is correct. The female appellant did not provide credible testimony pertaining to the allegations central to the refugee protection claims. The appeals are dismissed.

In accordance with Huruglica,1 the RAD carried out an independent review of the evidence submitted in support of the appeal, including the transcript of the two hearings in question. Furthermore, since the RPD did not enjoy a meaningful advantage as to the issue of credibility, it applied the correctness standard.

From its review of all the evidence, consisting of two hearings totalling more than 7 hours, 24 documentary exhibits submitted by the appellants, and 1 exhibit disclosed by the RPD, in addition to the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Mexico, the RPD made at least 15 adverse findings as to the female appellant's credibility. On appeal, only five of these are contested, relating to both incidents alleged to have occurred in 2014 and 2017-2018. Appellant's credibility regarding alleged incidents in XXXX 2014 Unsatisfactory justification for the contradictions and omissions raised by the RPD concerning the two written accounts produced by the female appellant

The appellants first argue that a satisfactory explanation was offered to the RPD to justify all the contradictions and omissions raised between the first and second written account appended to the Basis of Claim Forms (BOC Forms). The assistant of the appellants' first counsel was responsible for these numerous errors.

It is important to first note that the appellants submitted an initial written account appended to their BOC Forms on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018, approximately two weeks after their arrival in Canada. However, they submitted a new written account on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, 10 days before the first hearing. According to their counsel at the time of the RPD hearing, that is, their second counsel, this should be considered a new written account as it was completely rewritten and highlighted.

The RPD noted several contradictions between the first and second written statements: the date the female appellant's husband was kidnapped was changed, as was the amount of the ransom demanded; the manner in which police protection was sought and the ransom payment differed significantly.2 Second, the RPD noted that several elements omitted from the first written account were also omitted from the second written account: the fact that the female appellant and her daughter returned to the country for 20 months does not appear in the second written account or in the immigration forms, neither does a stay at a friend's house in XXXX 2018, and then in a hotel, nor their stay at the female appellant's brother's home prior to the appellants' departure to Canada. The RPD also noted that there was no mention of the fact that two employees of the shoe business owned by the female appellant and her husband were suspected of being complicit in the kidnapping and subsequent extortion.3

The RPD asked the female appellant to explain the contradictions and omissions identified when comparing the first and second written accounts submitted in support of the refugee protection claims. According to the female appellant, all of these errors were attributable to her previous counsel's assistant, who wrote a French version of her first written account that the female appellant signed without being able to read it and believing that her words had been accurately reported. It was only in XXXX 2019, when she had changed counsel, that she allegedly noticed the errors in her written account.

The RPD did not consider this explanation satisfactory because the female appellant stated that she had spent hours with this assistant, who also served as an interpreter to tell her story. The RPD disclosed the assistant's LinkedIn profile. According to this page, this woman is a graduate of Université de Montréal, has 20 years of experience working with immigrants, particularly in translation, and runs her own business in this regard. However, the panel cannot understand the connection between her and the appellants' first counsel. Given her experience and the female appellant's testimony as to the care she took in handling the refugee protection claims in this case, the RPD considered [translation] "it unreasonable to believe that the assistant would have inserted so many false allegations into the principal claimant's written account."4

The RAD cannot accept the arguments of the appellants, who claim that it is just as unreasonable to believe that the female appellant would have deliberately produced a written account so riddled with errors, and then elected to present a second written account supported by numerous documents, as it is to blame the errors in the first written account on the first counsel's assistant.

First, the female appellant confirmed that she met with this assistant several times, discussed her story with her at length and thought that she was a professional and a good listener. She felt confident. She also stated that in XXXX 2018, she gave her a written version of her story in Spanish. This makes sense given the female appellant's statement that the assistant did not take notes during their meeting.5 It is thus clear from the hearing that the female appellant provided an initial written version in order to help the assistant.

The RPD asked the female appellant if she had this first Spanish version of her written account with her. She clearly and spontaneously answered in the affirmative. When the RPD asked if it could see it, the female appellant again spontaneously answered in the affirmative.6 After the break, the RPD asked the female appellant if she had found the document. She initially stated that she had not found it and then explained that she had been mistaken and confused because the only version of her written account in Spanish was actually the second version submitted in XXXX 2020. Then she stated that she translated her written account using Google.7 It can only be understood from this last statement that she translated her written account from Spanish to French.

Ultimately, the female appellant adjusted her testimony so that there was only one Spanish version of her written account-the translated version submitted to the RPD in XXXX 2020, which she allegedly initially gave to her first counsel's assistant but also translated herself. Either her first counsel's assistant was behind the false allegations in her written account or Google provided such a poor translation that it resulted in the insertion of false allegations in the female appellant's written account.

In this context, the presumption in Maldonado8 is rebutted because, contrary to the appellants' statements in their memorandum, serious doubts are raised here as to the truthfulness of the allegations. The RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct. The explanations offered by the female appellant are not satisfactory and seriously undermine her credibility. Failure to include photographs of forced sexual acts in XXXX 2014

The appellants argue that the RPD erred in failing to apply Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution when it considered the omission of photographs of sexual acts by the female appellant during her husband's confinement. It allegedly did not show sensitivity to these incidents and did not consider the female appellant's explanations for their omission.

During the hearing, after the children had left the room, the female appellant disclosed to the RPD that in XXXX 2014, she was forced to photograph herself performing sexual acts and then send them to her husband's kidnapper. Out of respect for the female appellant, the RPD did not ask any questions about the content of these images or the context in which the photographs were taken. It simply asked the female appellant to explain why these incidents did not appear in the first or second written accounts or in the statement given to the police on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014.9 By way of explanation, the female appellant stated that in drafting her written account, what was important were the threats received in 2017. Regarding Exhibit D-11, her statement to the police dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, she stated that it was not complete because the police officers would not give her a full version of her statement. When asked to clarify her response due to the many pages and details in this statement, she stood by her answer and stated that there was a lot of information missing from this document, such as what happened after her husband was released. In light of this response, the RPD pointed out to the female appellant that this document was prepared on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, as evidenced by its contents, and gave the female appellant the opportunity to explain why it would contain her husband's statements if he had been released on or about XXXX XXXX. Ignoring the question, the female appellant stated that she went to the police many times. Lastly, the RPD gave the female appellant one last chance to clarify whether this document contained her statement of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, to which the female appellant responded in the affirmative.10

In the RPD's view, the female appellant did not offer an explanation for why she made no mention of the photographed forced sexual acts she allegedly performed during her husband's kidnapping. Instead, she sidestepped the subject by not offering clear answers to the RPD's straightforward questions. The RPD did not overlook the fact that this may have been a painful and embarrassing experience for the female appellant, or her explanations for her failure to mention this alleged experience to anyone. Rather, it analyzed them and concluded that they were unsatisfactory. The RPD followed the principles set out in Chairperson's Guideline 4 and was not insensitive in its treatment of this omission. The RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct. The female appellant's explanations are unsatisfactory and undermine her credibility. Contradictions between the female appellant's testimony and Exhibit D-11 (police report of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014)

In the appellants' view, the RPD erred in considering that the female appellant provided unsatisfactory explanations for the contradictions between her testimony and the contents of Exhibit D-11, the police report dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, in which she reported her husband's kidnapping. The appellants argue that the RPD failed to present sufficient reasons for not giving probative value to this document.

At the first hearing, the female appellant stated that she fears members of the La Famille Michoacán cartel, specifically a certain El Comandante [the commander], who allegedly kidnapped and held her husband captive, and that she suspected two former employees, XXXX and XXXX XXXX of having been accomplices in the kidnapping. The RPD pointed out to the female appellant that there is no mention of the cartel or a person who would answer to the title of commander, nor is there any mention of her suspicion regarding her former employees in her first statement to the police dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, filed as Exhibit D-11. The female appellant stated that she discussed this information with the police but did not know why they did not appear in the report. When asked why it was mentioned that she suspected a person named XXXX, a former employee arrested three months before the events, she replied that at the time of the kidnapping, she suspected him of being behind it.

The RPD did not consider the female appellant's explanations satisfactory as she previously stated that she feared the cartel, the commander, and XXXXandXXXX XXXX, without ever mentioning a person named XXXX. In addition, the RPD concluded that if a person fears a known and powerful cartel in Mexico and reports a kidnapping in this regard, it is reasonable to expect that this would be mentioned in a statement made to the police, which also contains a long and detailed statement. It drew the same conclusion concerning the female appellant's suspicions against her former employees.

The RAD is of the opinion that the RPD's conclusions are sufficiently substantiated. The RPD took the female appellant's explanations into account and did not consider them satisfactory, with good reason. The document only mentions the event, that is, the kidnapping and captivity of the female appellant's husband, the ransom demand and the suspicion against a former employee, all in detail, including the words exchanged during the various calls between the alleged kidnapper and the female appellant. Basic elements of the alleged police investigation, such as the name of the cartel, are not mentioned in the police report that forms the basis of the refugee protection claims in this case, and it is reasonable to expect that a police officer would mention this basic information in such a detailed statement. The RPD's conclusion is correct and the female appellant's credibility is undermined.

Based on the foregoing reasons, the RAD is of the view that the appellants have failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations regarding the events that reportedly took place in XXXX 2014, namely, that the female appellant's husband was kidnapped by members of the La Famille Michoacán cartel, held captive for two weeks and released for ransom. The female appellant also failed to show, on a balance of probabilities, that she was forced to photograph herself performing sexual acts and send them to her husband's kidnapper. The RPD did not breach procedural fairness by taking into account documents about which the female appellant was not questioned in depth

The appellants argue that the RPD breached procedural fairness by making negative inferences as to the credibility of their allegations after analyzing police reports submitted after the second hearing (exhibits D-20 to D-24).

At the first hearing, the female appellant stated that there were other police reports concerning the events of 2014 but that she could not obtain them. However, at the second hearing, she submitted five new exhibits consisting of documents from the preliminary investigation conducted by Mexican police officers, all written in Spanish and not accompanied by a translation into French or English.

These exhibits consist of a statement by the female appellant dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014, a statement by her husband made on the same day, two statements made by employees who allegedly brought the ransom, and a preliminary report concerning the investigation file dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2014.

The RPD asked the female appellant how she obtained these documents since at the previous hearing she had stated that she was unable to obtain any additional documents from the police. The female appellant replied that she obtained them from a friend, who has a friend whose niece is a lawyer. This lawyer allegedly obtained the police file covertly and photographed the documents presented. The female appellant allegedly received these documents by email. When questioned about the identity of these individuals, the female appellant was unable to provide their full names.

Like the RPD, the RAD does not consider this explanation satisfactory because if such a person had been so close to the female appellant as to take such risks in stealing police documents, it would have been reasonable to expect that she knows their name. The female appellant was able to give the full name of her friend but not the name of her friend's friend or her friend's niece, who allegedly risked everything to steal a six-year-old file from the Mexican police.

For this reason alone, the RAD would have given no probative value to documents D-20 to D-24. The RPD continued its analysis, however, noting that it was unable to question the female appellant about the significant issues raised on the merits of these documents, the French translation of which was eventually filed with the panel. The RAD is of the opinion that the RPD's concerns were legitimate as these documents raise numerous credibility issues. These issues should have been brought to the female appellant's attention if only by written notice allowing her to respond. However, in the specific context of this case, there is no basis for claiming a breach of procedural fairness, as the female appellant had ample opportunity to submit these documents since XXXX 2018 or to provide an explanation for their late submission. Furthermore, there is no requirement that refugee protection claimants be confronted with information that they themselves provided.11 Ultimately, the RPD's decision was based not only on credibility issues regarding the content of these documents, but also on their late disclosure and the unsatisfactory explanation offered by the female appellant as to how they were obtained.12 The RAD therefore concludes that there was no breach of procedural fairness, that the RPD's decision that these documents have little probative value and cannot remedy all of the unjustified credibility issues previously raised is correct. Female appellant's credibility regarding alleged incidents in 2017-2018

The RAD notes that several times during the two hearings, the female appellant mentioned that the events justifying her and her children's claims for refugee protection were those that occurred in the six months prior to their flight to Canada, from XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017, to XXXX 2018. In the RAD's view, even if their claims had been based specifically on these events, the appellants have not shown, on a balance of probabilities, that they were threatened by anyone with anything in Mexico, thereby justifying the rejection of their claims.

Due to significant contradictions in the dates of the threats, the manner in which her husband was allegedly threatened and where he was at the time of the initial threats, all attributed to a translation error by the female appellant, an explanation considered unsatisfactory by the RPD, the RPD found that the female appellant's credibility was undermined, particularly with respect to her allegation of threats in 2017 and 2018. The appellants are not contesting this finding and, upon review, the RAD considers the RPD's finding to be correct.

The appellants are also not contesting the RPD's conclusion that the appellants were intermittently in Puebla for four months, from XXXXtoXXXX XXXX 2018, without being threatened there, before leaving the country, which is not consistent with the behaviour expected of individuals who claim to fear for their lives. On review, the RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct.

Lastly, the appellants are not contesting the credibility findings or the probative value, generally not given, to the documents reviewed by the RPD in assessing the threats allegedly made in 2017 and 2018 (D-9; D-12; D-14). After analyzing the evidence, the RAD concludes that there is no basis for intervention in this regard.

Ultimately, the appellants are contesting only one RPD conclusion concerning the events of XXXX 2018. The appellants argue that the RPD failed to provide compelling reasons for giving little probative value to Exhibit D-19 showing the obscene messages and photographs received by the female appellant in XXXX 2018 while she was in Canada.

The female appellant disclosed at the first hearing that she received obscene messages and photographs on her Mexican cellphone in XXXX 2018 while in Canada. When she asked the caller to identify themself, she allegedly received a clue consisting of a photograph of Mexican peso banknotes and a necklace. This necklace was allegedly given by the female appellant to her husband's kidnappers in XXXX 2014. The female appellant therefore alleges that she was threatened by the same individuals belonging to the La Famille Michoacán cartel, in XXXX 2018.

The RPD asked the female appellant to explain why this incident did not appear in her second written account, submitted in XXXX 2020, knowing that it could not appear in the first written account produced on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The female appellant replied that in her second written account she only explained the events that occurred before the drafting of her first written account. The RPD did not consider these explanations reasonable as the female appellant submitted what she stated was a new written account 10 days before the first hearing and confirmed that her BOC Form was complete. There is no basis for stating that a refugee protection claimant who submits an amendment to their BOC Form must stick to the first version of their written account; otherwise, there would be no reason to amend it.

Furthermore, in order to corroborate her allegation, the female appellant submitted the obscene messages and photographs to the RPD on February 19, 2020, (Exhibit D-19) six days after the first hearing and seven days before the second hearing. However, as the RPD correctly pointed out, she did not attach either a translation or an explanation for the delay in submitting this document, which allegedly existed 18 months before the date of the first hearing.

The RPD nevertheless did admit Exhibit D-19, consisting of screenshots clearly showing obscene messages and photographs and dated XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The female appellant explained that she sent the screenshots to her brother, who allegedly sent them back to her, to justify why she could not submit them from her own WhatsApp account or telephone. Contrary to the appellants' assertion, the RPD considered this evidence and provided clear reasons for giving little probative value to this exhibit. It correctly pointed out that there is no evidence that these screenshots came from the female appellant's telephone or that the messages have any connection to the cartel. The RAD adds that although the messages are obscene, they do not contain any death threats. What is more, the female appellant never mentioned the necklace allegedly offered to the kidnappers, neither in her written accounts nor to the police.

For all of these reasons, the RAD considers that the RPD's decision is correct, Exhibit D-19 has no probative value and cannot remedy the previous credibility issues that were raised and not explained satisfactorily.

For all the foregoing reasons, the RAD, like the RPD, concludes that the appellants have not demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities, that they received death threats from anyone in 2017 and 2018. The Refugee Protection Division is not required to mention each piece of evidence in its analysis

As a final ground of appeal, the appellants argue that the RPD did not consider all the evidence but instead retained evidence that supported its analysis, refusing to consider the documents in their favour.

This argument is surprising, to say the least, since it is based on the premise that certain documents would have been able to support the appellants' allegations while others would have undermined their claim; yet these documents were all submitted by the appellants themselves. In addition, the appellants do not mention precisely which document was overlooked by the RPD. Thus, the alleged error in the RPD's decision is not specified, as required by the Refugee Appeal Division Rules, paragraph 3(3)(g).

It is settled case law that the RPD and the RAD are not required to refer to every piece of evidence submitted in support of a claim in their decision.13 The fact that a piece of evidence was not explicitly referenced and cited does not mean it was overlooked. It is clear from the RPD's decision that it considered all the evidence. What is more, so did the RAD. This ground of appeal is dismissed. Finding as to the female appellant's credibility

In their memorandum, the appellants generally argue that the RPD's analysis was too narrow, focusing on minor inconsistencies, whereas the female appellant had given clear, spontaneous and detailed testimony, accompanied by extensive evidence corroborating the allegations central to their claims.

The RAD disagrees. The RPD was patient with the female appellant, whose testimony was at times vague, confusing, evasive and unclear to questions that were clear and straightforward. In addition, while the evidence submitted was extensive, it failed to address the significant credibility issues raised by the RPD and the RAD.

Ultimately, for the above reasons, the RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct. The appellants have not established that if they were to return to Mexico, they would face a serious possibility of persecution or that they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, on a balance of probabilities.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the appeals are dismissed and the RPD's determination that the appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA is confirmed.
